createOrReplace.title: Core Sector Growth Hits 10.9% in October 2026
createOrReplace.html:
India's core sector growth hit 10.9% in October 2026, up from a revised 8.2% in September, according to provisional government data reported by DD News. Iron ore, coal and electricity led the gains. But October 2025 grew just 0.8%, so much of the jump is a low base. The steadier signal is cumulative April–October growth of 6.0%.

This matters now because core sector output feeds directly into the official industrial production numbers due at the end of the month, and into the cost and availability of the inputs every plant buys: power, steel, cement and fuel. The October print is the highest since the revised index was introduced in July 2026, Construction Mirror reports. For founders and operations heads planning Q4 production and FY27 budgets, the useful question is not "is 10.9% good?" but "how much of it is real demand?"

TL;DR

  • The Index of Core Industries grew 10.9% year on year in October 2026, against a revised 8.2% in September and a provisional 7.9% before revision.
  • Iron ore rose 26.4%, coal 23.1% and electricity 21.6%; cement added 15.4% and steel 7.3%.
  • Fertilisers fell 12.2%, natural gas 7.6% and crude oil 4.1%, so three of nine sectors contracted.
  • The base was weak: core output grew only 0.8% in October 2025, when coal fell 8.4% and electricity 7.0%.
  • April–October 2026 growth was 6.0%, against 2.3% a year earlier, the better gauge of momentum.

What did the October 2026 core sector data show?

It showed the fastest core sector growth of the revised series: 10.9% year on year, with six sectors growing and three contracting.

DD News, carrying the provisional data released by the commerce and industry ministry on 20 November, reports that the index rose to 123.1 in October 2026 from 111.0 a year earlier. September was revised up to 8.2% from a provisional 7.9%. Iron ore led at 26.4%, followed by coal at 23.1% and electricity at 21.6%. Cement grew 15.4%, steel 7.3% and refinery products 3.4%.

On the other side, fertiliser production fell 12.2%, natural gas 7.6% and crude oil 4.1%, Construction Mirror reports. Discovery Alert notes the natural gas fall was its steepest contraction in 31 months, and fertilisers have now declined for eight straight months. The index now covers nine sectors: the July 2026 revision moved the base year to 2022-23 and added iron ore, Construction Mirror reports.

Why did core sector growth jump to 10.9%?

Mostly because October 2025 was unusually weak, plus genuinely strong power and cement demand this year.

Core output grew just 0.8% in October 2025, Business Today reports. Discovery Alert explains that a shift in the festive calendar held that month down: coal output fell 8.4% and electricity dropped 7.0%. Compare a normal month against that hole and the growth rate looks large. Coal swung from an 8.4% fall to a 23.1% rise. Electricity went from a 7.0% decline to 21.6% growth.

ICRA chief economist Aditi Nayar called a good part of the growth "optical", as reported by Business Standard and summarised by Discovery Alert. She also pointed to elevated electricity demand and double-digit cement growth as real signals. Cement has now grown at double digits for four consecutive months, Discovery Alert reports. That is not a base effect: it reflects construction and infrastructure work on the ground.

Is the October surge real demand or a base effect?

Both. The headline is inflated by a weak base, but the month-on-month pickup from September and the cumulative 6.0% show real momentum.

Two checks help. First, compare with September, which had a normal base. September sector growth, per Business Today, was 18.4% for iron ore, 10.7% for coal, 12.6% for electricity, 10.1% for cement and 5.6% for steel. Every one of those accelerated in October. Refinery products went the other way, slowing from 8.7% to 3.4%.

Second, look at the cumulative figure. April–October 2026 growth was 6.0%, against 2.3% in the same period of 2025, DD News reports. Annual growth was 4.3% in 2024-25 and 3.0% in 2025-26. So FY27 is running about twice as fast as the last full year. Discovery Alert suggests treating 10.9% as an upper-bound monthly reading and 6.0% as the steadier gauge. ICRA expects growth to moderate to mid-single digits in November because of more holidays.

Which sectors matter most for the index?

Electricity, refinery products and steel, which together carry more than two-thirds of the weight, so their swings decide the headline.

Under the revised base, electricity carries 30.932% of the index, refinery products 22.572% and steel 17.584%, according to DD News. The smaller sectors are crude oil at 7.43%, coal at 5.596%, iron ore at 4.905%, cement at 4.41%, natural gas at 3.841% and fertilisers at 2.731%. That is why a 26.4% jump in iron ore moves the total far less than a 21.6% jump in electricity.

It also explains a quieter risk in the October number. Refinery products, the second-biggest weight, grew only 3.4%. If power demand normalises in November while refining stays soft, the headline can fall back quickly.

What does core sector growth mean for manufacturers and logistics firms?

It means input supply is healthy and costs for power, steel and cement are driven by demand rather than shortages, but planning should use the 6.0% trend, not the 10.9% spike.

For plant heads, the practical reads are specific. Strong cement and steel output, at 15.4% and 7.3% in October, point to an active construction and capital-goods pipeline, which means steady orders for suppliers to those sectors. The 21.6% rise in electricity output signals higher industrial and commercial load: check your demand charges and contract load before winter peaks. Falling fertiliser and natural gas output, down 12.2% and 7.6%, matter for agri-input distributors and gas-based process industries.

For logistics operators, coal and iron ore volumes, up 23.1% and 26.4%, are bulk rail and road freight. Higher volumes in these lanes can tighten rake and truck availability for everyone else, so watch transit times on routes that share capacity with mining belts.

How should operations leaders act on this data?

Treat it as a forecasting input, adjust for base effects, and wait for the October–November average before changing capacity plans.

  1. Plan on the trend, not the month. Use the 6.0% April–October growth as your baseline for FY27 volume planning, and treat 10.9% as a ceiling.
  2. Strip out calendar effects. A festive shift turned October 2025 into a 0.8% month. If your demand model compares raw year-on-year months, it will overreact the same way. Align by festival dates, not calendar months.
  3. Wait for two months. Economists cited by Construction Mirror say the October–November average gives the clearer picture. November data is due on 21 December, DD News reports.
  4. Map your exposure. List which of the nine core inputs your business buys or ships, and track only those sector lines each month.
  5. Automate the tracking. Pull the monthly release, your own sales and your supplier lead times into one view, so a 10.9% headline triggers a check, not a decision.

What this means for Indian businesses

The core sector data says the industrial base is growing faster this year than last: 6.0% against 2.3% for April–October. That is good news for manufacturers, construction suppliers and logistics firms. But the October headline is partly arithmetic, and businesses that plan on single-month spikes end up with excess inventory or idle capacity.

The fix is mostly about data hygiene. Most mid-sized firms still compare months in spreadsheets, without adjusting for festival timing or base effects. From the way we build forecasting and planning tools for Indian operators, the biggest gains come from joining public indicators like this index with a firm's own order book and supplier data, and flagging base effects automatically. Frequently asked questions

What is India's core sector growth for October 2026?

India's core sector growth was 10.9% year on year in October 2026, according to provisional data from the Office of the Economic Adviser reported by DD News. It is the highest reading since the revised index was introduced. September was revised up to 8.2%. The October figure may be revised next month.

What is the Index of Core Industries?

The Index of Core Industries measures monthly output in nine basic industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity and iron ore. In July 2026 the government moved its base year to 2022-23 and added iron ore. Electricity carries the largest weight, at 30.932%.

Why is the October 2026 growth called a base effect?

Because the comparison month was weak. Core output grew only 0.8% in October 2025, when a festive calendar shift cut coal output by 8.4% and electricity by 7.0%, Discovery Alert reports. Growth measured against that low base looks larger than the underlying change in activity.

Which core sectors contracted in October 2026?

Three of the nine sectors contracted in October 2026. Fertiliser output fell 12.2%, natural gas 7.6% and crude oil 4.1%, DD News reports. Discovery Alert adds that fertilisers have declined for eight consecutive months and natural gas had its steepest fall in 31 months.

Will core sector growth stay in double digits in November?

Probably not. ICRA expects core sector growth to moderate to mid-single digits in November 2026, mainly because the month has more holidays, according to Discovery Alert. The government is due to release November data on 21 December 2026, DD News reports, so the October–November average will give a cleaner read.
